title: Music therapy to improve the quality of life of patients with colorectal cancer undergoing adjuvant chemotherapy – a multicenter, randomized controlled intervention study
summary:
After colorectal cancer surgery, patients are usually recommended to undergo adjuvant chemotherapy with two drugs for at least three months. This treatment aims to reduce the risk of tumor recurrence. It is known that for at least one-third of patients, this therapy causes a significant decline in quality of life, which gradually improves back to the baseline (the state after surgery) over up to 12 months. Besides the physical impact and side effects of chemotherapy, social life and mental and emotional well-being can also be affected.
Engagement with music—whether through listening, making music, or interactions with music therapists—can provide valuable support during chemotherapy and help maintain or improve various symptoms, as studies have shown. A report by the Institute for Quality and Efficiency in Health Care (IQWiG) described evidence of short-term benefits of music therapy compared to standard care, including reductions in fatigue, mood swings, anxiety and depression, stress/tension, and improvements in health-related quality of life. Over multiple sessions, additional benefits were noted regarding disease-related adverse events, fatigue, and mood fluctuations. Other studies also report improved well-being, better quality of life, reduced anxiety, and relief from physical symptoms such as chronic fatigue in patients with cancer diagnoses.
This study is the first to systematically investigate and compare over three months the effects of two types of music interventions—music therapy or music medicine (i.e., music listening)—in patients starting adjuvant chemotherapy after colorectal cancer surgery. A total of 367 patients will participate, randomly assigned to three groups: one receiving only chemotherapy, the second receiving chemotherapy plus up to 12 sessions with a music therapist over three months, and the third group listening to provided music for about 15 minutes each evening.
The study aims to demonstrate that structured use of music improves quality of life and reduces symptoms. Additionally, it seeks to determine whether support from music therapists is superior to independently and regularly listening to relaxing music.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
- Age: ≥ 18 years
- Gender: all genders
- Diagnosis: Histologically confirmed, curatively resected colorectal carcinoma (stage II  or stage III)
- Therapy: Planned adjuvant chemotherapy for at least 3 months
Exclusion criteria:
- Age: Under 18 years
- Prior treatment: Current use of other music therapy and/or music medicine interventions or use of such interventions within the last three months before study entry, to exclude potential residual effects of previous interventions
- Language: Insufficient German language skills so that study information, music interventions, or questionnaires cannot be understood or completed
